title: Jeff Bezos sends a strong signal to Nvidia stock investors as CEO search heats up
detail:
Jeff Bezos sends a strong signal to Nvidia stock investors as CEO search heats up
Jean Christine, Aparajita Chatterjee
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 2:07 PM MST 5 min read
NVDA
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia has had exactly one CEO since 1993. Now it needs a second, and plenty of famous names in tech have opinions about who should get the job.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos is one of them. His advice matters to anyone whose 401(k) or index fund holds Nvidia stock, because he thinks the chipmaker's board should look inside the building before it looks anywhere else.

Bezos would keep the job in the family

"If you don't bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider," Bezos said at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference on Nov. 17. "Nvidia is too complicated."

He doesn't think much of a newcomer's odds.

"I think outside CEOs in complex companies have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding," Bezos said. "And so I would always think that's a last resort."

More Bezos: Jeff Bezos says 2 policies drive up housing costs, and it's 'not hard to figure out'

Bezos followed that advice himself at Amazon. He handed the CEO job to Andy Jassy, the longtime head of Amazon Web Services, in July 2021. Bezos called his exit a "multi-year planned transition," which is nothing like what Nvidia just went through.

Bezos stayed out of whether Huang should get his job back, saying he didn't know enough about what happened behind closed doors. He did have praise for Huang.

"Jensen is a remarkable guy who founded and built a remarkable company with a lot of hard work and foresight," Bezos said. "And he deserves admiration and respect no matter what, and that will never go away."

Jeff Bezos says hiring an outside CEO should be Nvidia's "last resort."Chesnot / Getty Images
Huang raised his hand and the board said no

Nvidia announced on Nov. 12 that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member, according to the company's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. He left after admitting to an extramarital affair. Chief financial officer Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones became the board's first-ever chair.

Read more:

Jeff Bezos says your family is 'not going to need' 2 paychecks thanks to AI

Warren Buffett told Jeff Bezos the real reason people don't just 'copy' his investing strategy to get rich

Jensen Huang was 'broken and shattered' in final hours as Nvidia CEO

On the same day Bezos spoke, Huang said he wanted back in.

"Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang wrote in a post on X Nov. 17. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

title: Jeff Bezos predicts Amazon will eventually 'go bankrupt' and shares 30-year rule behind it
detail:
Jeff Bezos predicts Amazon will eventually 'go bankrupt' and shares 30-year rule behind it
Jean Christine, Celine Provini
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 11:33 AM MST 5 min read
AMZN
Trade AMZN on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Founders usually talk about their companies like proud parents at a graduation. One of the richest men on the planet once stood in front of his own staff and talked about the funeral.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos gave that answer when an employee asked where the company was headed. He said Amazon would one day go under, and he had a number in mind for how long giants like it usually last.

"Amazon is not too big to fail," Bezos said at an all-hands meeting in Seattle in November 2018, according to a recording heard by CNBC. "In fact, I predict one day Amazon will fail. Amazon will go bankrupt. If you look at large companies, their lifespans tend to be 30-plus years, not a hundred-plus years."

That's the 30-year rule, and Bezos applied it to his own company.

More Bezos: Warren Buffett told Jeff Bezos the real reason people don't just 'copy' his investing strategy to get rich

Sears had just proved Bezos' point

The employee's question was about what Amazon could learn from recent retail bankruptcies like Sears, according to CNBC. The 132-year-old chain had filed for Chapter 11 weeks earlier, in October 2018. Toys "R" Us had shuttered its last U.S. stores that June.

Amazon was 24 at the time, founded in July 1994. By Bezos' own math, the company was already most of the way to its expiration date.

The data backs up his gloomy math. Companies on the S&P 500 in the late 1970s stayed on the index for an average of 30 to 35 years, according to growth strategy firm Innosight, which forecast that the figure would shrink to 15 to 20 years this decade.

Jeff Bezos said his goal was to prolong Amazon's demise for as long as possible.Natalie Fobes / Getty Images
Amazon's goal was never to live forever

So Amazon is mortal. So what? Bezos' answer was that the job isn't avoiding the end. It's pushing it back.

He told employees to "obsess over customers," according to CNBC.

"If we start to focus on ourselves, instead of focusing on our customers, that will be the beginning of the end," Bezos said. "We have to try and delay that day for as long as possible."

He had already spelled out what happens when a company stops doing that.

"Day 2 is stasis," Bezos wrote in his 2016 letter to shareholders, published in April 2017. "Followed by irrelevance. Followed by excruciating, painful decline. Followed by death. And that is why it is always Day 1."

Day 1 meant acting like a startup that has to earn every customer, even at a company Amazon's size. In the same letter, Bezos pointed to Prime as proof. "No customer ever asked Amazon to create the Prime membership program, but it sure turns out they wanted it," he wrote.

title: Amazon.com vs. Home Depot: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Amazon.com vs. Home Depot: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Seena Hassouna, The Motley Fool

AMZN
HD
Explore stocks on Coinbase

How do you choose between a technology titan and a physical retail leader? Both Amazon.com (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Home Depot (NYSE:HD) offer investors unique exposure to consumer spending patterns and logistics expertise.

Amazon.com relies on its massive scale and digital ecosystem to drive growth across retail and cloud computing. Home Depot focuses on the home improvement market, serving both casual DIYers and professional trade specialists. This comparison helps you evaluate which strategy offers the best potential for the coming years.

The case for Amazon.com

Amazon.com operates a vast ecosystem that includes online and physical stores, third-party seller services, and advertising. The company serves a diverse customer base ranging from individual shoppers to large enterprises seeking cloud computing through Amazon Web Services. Its business model relies heavily on a network of third-party sellers and suppliers, many of which are based in China, to maintain its broad inventory.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $797.5 billion. This performance represents revenue growth of approximately 15.4% compared to the previous twelve-month period. Net income reached about $134.8 billion, but roughly $69 billion of that came from non-operating items, mostly gains on its private AI investments.

Based on its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 1.1x. This metric measures a company's ability to meet its short-term liabilities using assets that can be converted to cash within a year. The debt-to-equity ratio is about 0.4x, indicating the relationship between total debt and shareholders' equity. In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, free cash flow was negative roughly $47 billion, as equipment purchases outpaced operating cash flow.

The case for Home Depot

Home Depot is the leading name among retail stocks focused on home improvement. The company serves do-it-yourself consumers and professional contractors, such as general contractors and trade specialists. Following its acquisition of SRS, the company has expanded its specialized distribution capabilities to better serve the complex needs of professional building product customers.

In the 12 months ended Nov. 1, 2026, revenue reached approximately $171.2 billion. This represents revenue growth of nearly 3% as the company navigates shifts in consumer spending on home projects. Net income during the same period was roughly $14.3 billion, demonstrating steady profitability despite a slower growth environment than the technology sector.

Investors choosing between growth and stability often weigh the explosive potential of cosmetics against the steady demand for energy drinks. This comparison evaluates whether e.l.f. Beauty (NYSE:ELF) or Monster Beverage (NASDAQ:MNST) is the better buy.

e.l.f. Beauty disrupts the traditional makeup industry by offering high-speed product innovation and prestige-quality items at accessible prices. Monster Beverage dominates the beverage coolers with its diverse energy portfolio and global scale. Both companies have delivered impressive long-term results, but they offer distinct risk and reward profiles for retail investors.

The case for e.l.f. Beauty

e.l.f. Beauty operates in the competitive segment of consumer staples stocks, focusing on high-quality cosmetics at accessible price points. The company sells its products through mass, drug, and specialty retail channels, including key partners like Target (NYSE:TGT), Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT), and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN). These retail relationships account for nearly 76% of net sales, and such customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $1.9 billion. This represented revenue growth of roughly 39.9% compared to the prior twelve-month period. Net income for those 12 months was approximately $86.6 million, supported by a net margin of close to 4.5%.

As of its March 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.8x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity to show how a company funds its operations. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term debts with short-term assets, is close to 2.3x. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, free cash flow was nearly $190.1 million. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 40.9% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Monster Beverage

Monster Beverage functions as a holding company for major energy brands like Reign, NOS, and Bang. It primarily distributes its beverages through an extensive network of bottlers, relying on Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO) as its primary global distribution partner. The company currently serves a growing number of international markets across 80 countries, leveraging this massive network to maintain its market lead.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached close to $9.6 billion. This reflects revenue growth of approximately 20.2% over the previous year. Net income for the period was nearly $2.2 billion, resulting in a healthy net margin of approximately 22.7%.

title: Why Saturday’s Historic Starship Catch Changes the Bull Case for SpaceX Stock
detail:
Why Saturday’s Historic Starship Catch Changes the Bull Case for SpaceX Stock
Geoffrey Seiler, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 11:50 AM MST 5 min read
SPCX
AMZN
BA
LMT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

This past weekend was a big one for the space sector, with Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) showing it's light-years ahead of its competition. For the first time, SpaceX successfully caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket using mechanical arms attached to its launch tower. It was a major milestone for the company, setting the stage for its future space ambitions.

Also this weekend, rival United Launch Alliance (ULA), a joint venture between Boeing (NYSE:BA) and Lockheed Martin (NYSE:LMT), had a major setback. Its Vulcan rocket failed, destroying 40 Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) Leo satellites in the process.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

This weekend's results show the growing distance that SpaceX is gaining over its competitors in the space sector. Its achievement also comes months after Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket exploded on the ground in May, destroying the company's only launch pad. Space competitors are clearly struggling with launches, which is also hurting Amazon's efforts to get its Leo satellite internet service, which will compete with Amazon's Starlink, off the ground.

Still, not everything went well for SpaceX this weekend. It decided to abandon trying to catch Starship's Super Heavy booster, which it diverted to the Gulf of Mexico, where it exploded before reaching the water.

The Super Heavy Booster is the much more expensive part of Starship. According to PayLoad Research, a Starship rocket costs around $90 million, with the Super Heavy booster making up about $63 million of the total. However, the Super Heavy Booster is the easier part of the rocket to catch, and SpaceX has already caught it on its own multiple times.

Image source: SpaceX.

A space monopoly

Having a fully reusable rocket is paramount for SpaceX to achieve some of its loftier goals, like orbital data centers and Earth-to-Earth cargo transport. By rapidly reusing a $90 million rocket multiple times rather than just once, SpaceX not only saves a lot of money but also greatly increases the number of launches it can perform.

This completely changes the economics of space and sets the company up for strong growth and the ability to disrupt industries, essentially shifting SpaceX's space segment from being a low-margin launch business into a scalable logistics business, where fuel and maintenance are the main recurring costs.

Key Takeaways

A firm that manages $1.61 billion added to Amazon, Union Pacific and Marriott International in the third quarter, the three biggest positions it added to, according to its latest 13F.

Amazon is now the fund's largest holding, though at 2.7% of its 13F stocks, no single bet dominates.

Analysts' average price targets sit 32% above Amazon's latest close, 15% above Union Pacific's and just 4% above Marriott's.

Amazon looks like the best of the three buys to follow, for investors who can live with another year of heavy AI spending.

A fund doesn't have to be famous to be worth a look, especially when it's putting more money into stocks you probably already own. Sone Capital Management, which manages $1.61 billion, filed its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30 on Nov. 16, and the three biggest positions it added to were Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ), Union Pacific (UNP:NYSE) and Marriott International (MAR:NASDAQ).

The fund held 101 positions worth $1.42 billion at quarter-end prices, so none of these is a huge bet on its own. But they're now its first, third and fourth largest holdings.

Amazon is the fund's biggest bet, and Wall Street still likes it

The fund ended September with 154,902 Amazon shares, 36% more than three months earlier. They were worth $39 million, or 2.7% of its 13F stocks. The stock is down 0.9% since Sept. 30 and sits 14% below its 52-week high.

Not every big investor agrees. Third Point's Dan Loeb sold out of Amazon in the same quarter, arguing that AI spending is running far ahead of the revenue needed to pay for it. And CEO Andy Jassy has said Amazon will spend "meaningfully more" than this year's roughly $220 billion next year. Analysts now expect a $41.2 billion free cash outflow in 2026.

Analysts haven't backed off much, though. Their average price target rose from $294 to $327 over the past year:

Amazon.com (AMZN): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

That average sits 32% above the latest close, with individual targets running from $230 to $405.

Union Pacific keeps hauling more freight

The fund added 31% to its Union Pacific stake, ending September with 125,490 shares worth $34 million, 2.4% of its 13F stocks. The stock is up 6% since then.

The railroad gave it good reason in October. Third-quarter revenue rose 15% to $7.2 billion on 6% more carloads, pricing gains and a higher fuel surcharge, and adjusted EPS climbed 15% to $3.53. CEO Jim Vena also said Union Pacific looks forward to the next steps in the Surface Transportation Board's review of its merger with Norfolk Southern, which he pitches as America's first transcontinental railroad.

Key Takeaways

Anthropic's stock closed Friday 20% below its debut-day open, a hit to Amazon's stake of about 15% and Alphabet's 13.7%.

Gil Luria says Anthropic drove all of the recent acceleration in AWS and Google Cloud, which makes it a risk to both companies' revenue growth.

Anthropic's cash covers next year's commitments, so the real risk is that its spending grows more slowly.

A data-center builder that borrows heavily has the same exposure with less room for error, and Amazon's and Alphabet's fourth-quarter reports are the next test.

Anthropic (ANT:NASDAQ) gave back most of its first-day pop in two sessions. The stock opened at $111.50 on Thursday, 34% above its $83 IPO price, and closed Friday at $88.91.

That slide matters to Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) and Alphabet (GOOG). Per Anthropic's S-1, Amazon owns about 15% of Anthropic after the IPO and Alphabet owns 13.7%.

On Wednesday's episode of CNBC's Fast Money, D.A. Davidson's Gil Luria put Amazon and Google at the top of the list of companies tied to Anthropic, because "the entire acceleration in AWS and Google Cloud has come from Anthropic."

Whether the AI labs can keep paying for more compute matters to CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) too, since it borrows heavily to build data centers for them.

Much of the growth comes from one customer

Analysts expect Amazon's revenue growth to pick up, from 12% in 2025 to 16% this year and next, and 17% in 2028:

Amazon (AMZN): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

AWS revenue grew 37% in the second quarter, against 17% a year earlier. In that same quarter, Anthropic added more than $100 billion of AWS commitments over 10 years, per Amazon's 10-Q.

Analysts see an even steeper climb at Alphabet, from 15% revenue growth in 2025 to 24% this year and 27% in 2027:

Not all of that comes from Google Cloud. But by one tally of Anthropic's deals posted on X, Anthropic has committed at least $121.3 billion to it.

Amazon is spending ahead of that demand. Its free cash flow fell to $7.7 billion in 2025, from $32.9 billion in 2024:

Over the twelve months to June, it turned into a $7.6 billion outflow. Management expects about $220 billion of capital spending this year.

Amazon is also lending Anthropic part of what it spends on AWS. Per Amazon's 10-Q, $15 billion remained at June 30 on a $20 billion facility that becomes available to Anthropic as AWS delivers compute. If Anthropic slows its buying, Amazon is left holding capacity it has already paid for.

Citi Says SpaceX's Launch Lead Is "Increasingly Becoming a 20 Year Advantage." Starlink Is Where It Pays Off ©U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley and SUMALI IBNU CHAMID from Alemedia.id via Canva
Key Takeaways

Citi says SpaceX's launch lead is growing from a 10-to-15-year advantage to a 20-year one after its tower caught a Starship upper stage.

Starlink's operating margin rose to 40.7% in the first nine months of 2026 even as its average revenue per subscriber fell.

Amazon and AST SpaceMobile still need other companies' rockets, and Rocket Lab is years from SpaceX's scale.

The main risk is compute, which drives most of SpaceX's expected growth.

SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) caught a Starship upper stage with its launch tower for the first time, and Citi says the rest of the launch industry is falling further behind.

That's bad news for Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) and AST SpaceMobile (ASTS:NASDAQ), which both need someone's rockets to take on Starlink. It's also bad news for Rocket Lab (RKLB:NASDAQ), the closest public launch rival.

In a note on Nov. 16, Citi wrote that the "launch technology gap is widening," and that "a 10 to 15 year advantage is increasingly becoming a 20 year advantage."

The rockets are the small part

For shareholders, though, launch is a small part of SpaceX. On the Nov. 19 episode of 20VC, Rory O'Driscoll of Scale Venture Partners said the rockets "make the Starlink," but "most of the business and most of the market cap and most of the TAM, according to their own S1, is all about compute."

Analysts expect SpaceX's revenue to climb from $49.0 billion in 2026 to $336 billion in 2028:

SpaceX (SPCX): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2026-2028 (TIKR)

Compute is already driving that growth. The Super Intelligence segment brought in $7.56 billion of SpaceX's $14.6 billion of third-quarter revenue, and $6.75 billion of the $9.00 billion increase from a year earlier.

Cheap rides, rising Starlink margins

SpaceX gets the most out of its launch lead when it's flying its own satellites: 23 of its 35 launches in the third quarter carried its own payloads. You can't see that in SpaceX's total margin, though. Its operating margin went from 5.3% in 2024 to -11.1% in 2025, and those figures include the AI business it merged with in February:

SpaceX (SPCX): operating (EBIT) margin (%), fiscal 2023-2025 (TIKR)

The AI side lost $6.4 billion from operations in 2025. Starlink's Connectivity segment, meanwhile, earned $5.21 billion of GAAP operating income in the first nine months of 2026, a 40.7% margin, up from 38.6% a year earlier. (The third quarter got a one-time boost, mainly from tariff refunds.)
